new_statements.quote: Both the neutral tone and stress accent are tied to a single syllable, particularly a syllable core. However, although this explanation can function practically in Lhasa Tibetan, it has not been applied to Lamo; no linguistic realisation supports either the existence or non­existence of stress on a single syllable. [...] In summary, the formulation of Lamo's suprasegmental phenomenon is essentially common to the Kansai (Keihan) Japanese system: a combination of the height at a word-initial position (H or L) and the existence of an accent nucleus between two given syllables (falling point).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lamo is described as a tone language, not a stress language: every word carries a two-way H (high-level/high-falling) vs L (low-rising) contrast located at the word-initial position, plus an optional 'accent nucleus' (a falling point, written with an apostrophe) between the first and second syllables which makes the second syllable atonal/low. The tone-bearing unit is only the first two syllables of the phonological word; third and later syllables are atonal (low level), and most suffixes fall outside the TBU. Disyllabic patterns are HH, LH, H'L, L'L (Table 1, p. 70). The authors explicitly state that no phonetic or phonological evidence supports either the existence or the non-existence of stress on any single syllable, so no stress position can be assigned; they liken the system to the Kansai Japanese accent-nucleus system rather than to Tibetic stress accent (Caplow 2016), while deliberately avoiding the label 'pitch accent' (p. 81 notes Ikeda 2002 and Ding 2001 use that term for similar systems in Darmdo Minyag and Prinmi). A reviewer could alternatively code this as 'pitch accent'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; no stress of any kind is posited. Only the first two syllables bear tone, all later syllables are atonal (low).
new_statements.exceptions: Minimal pairs for tone and for the accent nucleus are rare (pp. 70-71). Tonal assignment of numerals varies across the four varieties (Kyilwa, Gewa, Sitsekha, Roba; Table 2 and Table 4, pp. 72-78), e.g. Kyilwa has H on 'eleven'-'seventeen' but L on 'eighteen'-'twenty'. In numeral compounds (21-99, 100+), each numeral morpheme keeps its own TBU and the linker /phe/ is atonal [L]; some speakers pronounce every suffix-like morpheme low regardless (p. 73). Preaspiration correlates with H but can co-occur with L (p. 70). Some speakers have shifted vowels so that the nucleus in the base form must be lexically registered (pp. 71-72).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the TBU is the phonological word (root plus affixes) limited to its first two syllables; described from elicited citation forms and numeral constructions collected from 14 speakers of both dialects (lDongpa Lamo incl. Kyilwa/Gewa/Phukha; Lamei incl. Sitsekha/Roba/Wamei), with the Kyilwa variety used for the system description in sec. 2.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source describes Lamo proper, primarily the Kyilwa variety of the lDongpa (Dongba Township) dialect, with data from 14 speakers covering both dialects, lDongpa Lamo (Kyilwa, Gewa, Phukha) and Lamei (Sitsekha, Roba, Wamei; Zhonglinka Township). Glottolog 5.3 files all of these plus the closely related gSerkhu variety (Dzayul County) under lamo1245 (hh language code 'gSerkhu = Lamo'); Glottolog 5.3 has since placed Lamo in a 'Chamdoic' group (cham1336) with Larong sMar (Zlarong) and Drag-yab sMar, whose suprasegmentals the same paper also treats. Chinese sources call the language Dongba hua 东坝话.

sources.note: Whole paper is on Lamo suprasegmentals: tone language with H vs L at word-initial position plus an 'accent nucleus' between syllables 1 and 2; TBU = first two syllables, later syllables atonal (p. 69-70, Table 1).
